sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does every element, rule, box, and ornament do a job, so that removing it would lose something?** No. Each of the three cards (x 56–416, 440–800, 824–1184; y 72–632) is about 560 px tall, but its text ends around y 330. That leaves about 300 px of plain orange, green, or purple at the bottom of every card, over half the box. Viewers read this as something missing: a photo that didn't load, or a button or timetable link that should sit there. The cards look unfinished, and the reader's next step has nowhere to go. Nothing on the piece says when, how much, or where to click, so the empty space sits exactly where the ask would be. The empty boxes are more noticeable than the content. This is a defect, argued from common sense: Rams ("every ornament does a job") and Tschichold ("negative space is deliberate") are off the approved reading list or name the rule only in general terms. To fix it, either fit the cards to their content or fill the lower area with what the visitor needs to act: the session time or price, and one specific link per card (for example "See Tuesday classes"). If a picture was meant to go there, check that it loads. Weight: major.

**What's working.**
- The headings name what each card offers in plain words a stranger understands at once: "Learn to swim", "Join the lanes", "Family hour". Each one-line body names who it's for, when it runs, and what's there ("every morning from six, with three speeds"), so the one-sentence purpose (a pool's three swim programmes, one per type of swimmer) comes through in seconds.
- The three cards share one type style, one corner radius, one padding, and one text layout. They differ only in hue, so they read as one set of equal options, and the colour on its own separates the programmes.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 7 yes, 1 no (every element does a job)

sections.report:
**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does one element stand clearly above the rest, by size or by contrast, so the eye knows where to start?** No. There are three cards at x 56–416, 440–800 and 824–1184 (all y 72–632). They're the same size and shape, with the same ~52 px bold white headlines, the same body text, and three saturated fills (rust, green, purple) of about the same strength. There's no page title, intro or other element above or around them. The eye lands on the left card only because people read left to right, then moves sideways through three equal blocks. The viewer can't tell what the page is (it reads as a swimming pool's programmes) or which programme matters most. Each card's lower ~300 px (y ~330–632) is empty colour, so the strongest thing on the page is three big slabs of colour, not any message.
   - **Why:** Tschichold (*The New Typography*) says order should be shown by differences of size. Hofmann (*Graphic Design Manual*) builds a composition from contrasts such as much against little. Here all the main elements are the same size, so the page has no contrast of scale.
   - **Fix:** Make one element clearly the first thing seen and set the rest back. If the three programmes really are peers, keep the cards equal but add one dominant element above them: a page heading that says what this is and who it's for. If one programme matters most, give it a larger card or the only strong fill, and quieten the other two.
   - **Kind and weight:** Defect, because the viewer has to work out what the page is and where to start. Also a convention, since it breaks Tschichold and Hofmann. Major.

**What's working.**
- Inside each card the text has two clearly separate levels. The headline is about 2.7× the size of the body (~52 px against ~19 px) and also bold against regular, so headline and description never get confused.
- The headlines are short, concrete phrases ("Learn to swim", "Join the lanes", "Family hour"). With the bold weight, each card is easy to tell apart once the eye is on it.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 2 yes, 1 no (one element dominates)

sections.report:
**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Is the empty space gathered into a few deliberate areas, rather than left over in scattered small gaps?** No. Each of the three cards (about x 56–416, 440–800 and 824–1184, y 72–632) is about 560 px tall, but its heading and three lines of body text end near y 330. The bottom 300 px of every card, more than half its height, is flat colour with nothing in it. The viewer sees three tall coloured slabs with the content stuck to the top. The empty half doesn't read as a resting place set against dense text. It reads as leftover, as if the cards were sized for content that never arrived: a missing picture, a time, a price, or a button. Each of these offers is something to sign up for, but nothing tells the viewer what to do next, and the empty space makes that gap obvious. Ruder (*Typography: A Manual of Design*, "Contrasts", "Form and counter-form") asks for empty space that stands in deliberate tension with the filled areas. Here it is the same dead block repeated three times. Fix: either size the cards to their content, so they end a comfortable padding below the text, or fill the lower part with what each offer needs, such as when it runs, who it's for and how to book, with the action pinned to the bottom of the card. If the cards must stay tall, make the empty area clearly intended, for example with a large picture or a bottom-anchored action. If a picture or button failed to load, the space would be fine; see below. Defect. Weight: major.
2. **Does the visual weight balance, with no side, crowded or empty, that makes the page look about to tip?** No. The row of cards sits left and high in the 1280×800 frame. The left margin is about 56 px and the right about 96 px. The top margin is 72 px and the bottom about 168 px. Inside each card all the weight is also at the top. The page leans up and to the left: the margins are too close to equal to look chosen and too far apart to look centred, so the placement looks accidental (Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, ch. I "Balance"). Fix: centre the row in the frame with equal side margins, or align it clearly to a page grid that other content shares. Also deal with the empty space inside the cards (finding 1), which causes most of the top-heaviness. Defect, though slight. Weight: minor.

**What's working.** The three cards are built on one strict system: equal widths of about 360 px, one gutter of about 24 px, the same 32 px inner padding, headings that break to two lines in every card, and body text that starts on the same line (about y 256) in all three. The row reads as one evenly spaced set of three equal choices. In each card the heading sits close to its own paragraph, and the cards are clearly separated, so it's obvious which text belongs to which offer. Keep both the system and that grouping when you change the card heights.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** The empty lower half of each card looks like the place for a picture or a button. If something there failed to load or is hidden by an animation, finding 1 changes from "the layout leaves dead space" to "fix the capture". Check it in a live browser. I also couldn't see how the row reflows at narrower widths.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 11 yes, 2 no (white space gathered, not scattered; visual weight balances).

sections.report:
**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do headings and captions break at phrase boundaries, never between a number and its unit or inside a name?** The heading breaks fall inside the phrase. On the left card (about x 88–300, y 110–220) "Learn to / swim" separates "to" from its verb. On the middle card (about x 472–680, y 110–220) "Join the / lanes" leaves "the" hanging at the end of the first line. Each heading takes a slight double-take, because the first line ends on a function word and reads as unfinished ("Learn to…", "Join the…"). "Family / hour" on the right card breaks cleanly, so the three cards also don't match each other. **Taste / common sense**: the catalog entry's only confirmed source (Bringhurst 2.4.6) is about numbers and units. Breaks inside headings are not covered by a confirmed source. **Fix:** break at the phrase ("Learn / to swim", "Join / the lanes"), or keep each phrase together with a non-breaking space, so every first line ends on a word that carries meaning. **Weight: minor.**

**What's working.**
- **Contrast and sizes:** white type on the saturated cards reads cleanly. By eye, the contrast is about 5.2:1 on the orange (#C2410C), 5.0:1 on the green (#15803D) and 6.9:1 on the purple (#7E22CE), which clears 4.5:1 even for the ~18 px blurbs. Keep the cards at this depth or darker if the colours change, because a lighter tint of any of them would drop below the line.
- **One type family, two clearly different levels:** a heavy, tightly spaced display heading with tight leading, over a regular-weight blurb at roughly a third of its size. The two levels never get confused. The blurbs are short (3 lines, about 30 characters per line), set flush left with an even rag and no stranded last words.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 29 yes, 1 no (headings break at phrase boundaries)

sections.report:
You asked me to follow section-critic.md for the color section. Bash was blocked in this session, so I couldn't run `scripts/crop.mjs` or `scripts/entries.mjs`. The image is about one screen (around 1280×800), so I judged it from the whole image and read the checklist entries directly from `references/color.md`.

**Section.** Color: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does the piece use a small palette, about one neutral range and one or two hues besides the status colors?** and **Is strong, saturated color kept to a small share of the area, with most of the area neutral or muted?** These are one problem.
   - **Where:** The three cards, at about x 56–416, 440–800 and 824–1184, y 72–632. Each is a fully saturated fill in a different, unrelated hue: burnt orange-red, green and violet. White is the only neutral. Together the cards cover roughly 60% of the canvas, so most of the area is vivid color.
   - **What the viewer meets:** Three vivid colors of the same size and strength, and none leads. The eye has no clear starting card. The palette looks picked one card at a time rather than from a system. The fills are flat and fully saturated, and there is little else on the page, so the color is the loudest thing here. It tires the eye more than it guides it.
   - **Why:** Itten, *The Art of Color*, says that in a three-hue scheme one hue leads and the others are muted, and that three equally saturated hues at equal weight is a defect. Refactoring UI asks for a small, defined palette ("Define your shades"), with saturated color kept to what matters.
   - **Fix:** Choose one lead color, ideally the brand color. Either give all three cards that hue, or turn the cards into light tints or neutrals and keep the strong color for a small accent per card, such as a button or a rule. If the three programmes really need their own colors, keep the hues but mute them to tints so no single card shouts.
   - **Type and weight:** Defect, major.
2. **Do warm colors sit on what should come forward and cool ones on what should recede?**
   - **Where:** The orange-red "Learn to swim" card (x 56–416) is the only warm hue.
   - **What the viewer meets:** That card comes forward and is seen first. The green and violet cards next to it fall back. Nothing on the page says this programme is the priority; the layout treats the three as equals.
   - **Why:** Itten, *The Art of Color*, on warm and cool contrast.
   - **Fix:** If one programme should lead, give the warm hue to that one on purpose. If they are equal, use colors of matching temperature, or one hue for all three.
   - **Type and weight:** Convention, minor.
3. **Is each status color (red, green, amber, blue) used only for its usual meaning to this audience?**
   - **Where:** The red-leaning orange (x 56–416) and the green (x 440–800) are status colors, and here they only decorate.
   - **What the viewer meets:** Side by side, red then green faintly suggests stop and go, or closed and open. That is a small risk on a page offering times and sessions, where "Learn to swim" might be read as unavailable.
   - **Why:** Apple HIG "Color" and Material Design color roles both say not to use status colors as unrelated decoration.
   - **Fix:** Move the first card off red-orange, or avoid using red and green together as decoration.
   - **Type and weight:** Convention, minor.

**What's working.**
- **The dark-light structure survives grayscale.** All three fills are mid-dark under bold white headings and white body text, so figure and ground still read with the color removed. The white text looks to clear 4.5:1 on all three fills, though the orange and green are closest; measure them.
- **No vibrating edges.** The cards are kept apart by white gutters (about 24 px), so no two strong hues touch and nothing shimmers.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 6 yes, 3 no (small palette and little saturated area as one finding; warm forward, cool back; status colors only for their meaning)

sections.report:
**Walk (working notes).** The first read: three tall, saturated cards, orange, green and purple, each with a large white imperative headline ("Learn to swim", "Join the lanes", "Family hour") and two or three lines of body text. The bottom ~55% of each card is empty. I read this as a leisure centre or pool's "ways to swim" section on a web page. The image is 1280×800, about one screen, so no crops are needed. Controls: none are visible, but the cards present themselves as calls to action (imperative headlines on tile-shaped blocks), so I'm walking the section.

1. One primary action: **no**. No action is styled at all, so there is no button on any card.
2. Controls look like what they do: **no**. If the cards are clickable, nothing says so: no button, arrow, underline or "Book" label.
3. Non-text contrast 3:1: yes (all three card fills look well above 3:1 against white).
4. States: yes (none shown). 5. Focus indicator: **unsure** (still). 6. Focus not obscured: yes. 7. Content uncovered: yes. 8. Target size: yes (cards are about 360×560). 9. Phone reach: yes (desktop). 10. System status: yes (this is a section fragment). 11. Way out: yes. 12–13: yes. 14. Recognition: yes. 15. Progressive disclosure: yes. 16–21 forms and errors: yes (none). 22. Empty state: yes. 23. Help: yes. 24. Shortcuts: yes.
25. Anticipation: **no**. The card doesn't give the next thing the viewer needs (exact times, price, how to book), and the empty lower half is where that would go.
26–33: yes.

The Bash tool was denied in this session, so I couldn't run `crop.mjs` or `entries.mjs`. I'm working from the whole image and the checklist line wording.

---

**Section.** Interface: applies. No control is visible, but the three cards are written as calls to action, so whether and how they can be acted on is the interface question.

**Findings**
1. **Is exactly one button styled as the primary action, with every other action styled lower? / Does every control look like what it does, buttons pressable, fields typeable, and links marked by more than color?** Where: all three cards (x 56–416, 440–800, 824–1184; y 72–632).
   - **What the viewer meets:** Each headline is an imperative ("Learn to swim", "Join the lanes"). That invites the viewer to act, but there is nothing to act on: no button, no "Book a class →" link, no arrow or chevron. If the whole card is a link, a still gives no sign of it, so the viewer has to guess and hover to find out. If the cards aren't links, the invitation stops dead and the viewer has to look for booking somewhere else.
   - **Why:** Buttons and links must look clickable (Norman's signifiers; Krug, *Don't Make Me Think*).
   - **Fix:** Give each card one visible, labelled action in the same place at the bottom of the card, such as "Book a class", "See lane times" or "Plan a visit", styled the same on all three because the three offers are equal. If the whole card stays clickable, keep that, but still show the cue. What would make this fine: a visible link cue on each card.
   - Defect. Weight: **major**.
2. **Does the screen put what the user likely needs next in front of them (a prefilled default, the next action, or the information they came for) instead of making them hunt for it?** Where: the lower half of each card, roughly y 340–632, which is empty.
   - **What the viewer meets:** The copy gets halfway to a decision. "Tuesday evenings" has no time. "Every morning from six" has no end time. "Sunday afternoons" has no hours. No card gives a price or says whether you need to book. A viewer who is interested has to go and find those facts before they can decide, and the space to hold them is already sitting empty.
   - **Why:** Tognazzini's anticipation principle. The source is off the reading list, so treat this as common sense.
   - **Fix:** Use the empty lower half for the two or three facts each viewer acts on (time, price, booking needed or drop-in), placed just above the action from finding 1.
   - Taste/common sense. Weight: **minor**.

**What's working.** The cards are very large targets (about 360×560 px each), so if they're clickable they're easy to hit with a mouse or a thumb. Each card fill also stands out from the white page well above 3:1, so each card's edge reads clearly as one object.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Whether the cards are clickable, and if so whether they have hover and focus states. A focus ring has to show on top of saturated orange, green and purple fills, so check in a live browser that it reaches 3:1 against both the card and the white page.

**Checklist.** Interface: 33 lines, 29 yes, 3 no (exactly one primary action; controls look like what they do; next need anticipated), 1 unsure (focus indicator)
